payload.channelWideVisualApproach: Evidence-led cinematic historical reconstruction that keeps factual confidence, reconstruction, and uncertainty visually distinguishable while preserving continuity across a long-form-first production.
realismAndFactualityPrinciples: Prefer historically plausible people, spaces, objects, materials, clothing, and environmental conditions over decorative fantasy.
Do not present a generated reconstruction as if it were an authenticated primary source, archival photograph, portrait, map, document, or artifact.
When the script expresses uncertainty, the image language must preserve that uncertainty rather than convert it into visual certainty.
Visual drama may clarify attention and emotion, but must not invent a decisive historical fact that the approved story context does not support.

characters: Recurring people keep stable age range, facial identity, body proportions, hair/headwear logic, status cues, and period-appropriate wardrobe identity unless an approved state change requires a revision.
Temporary emotion, pose, dirt, injury, weather exposure, and scene-specific costume details remain contextual and must not overwrite locked identity.
locations: Recurring locations keep stable architecture, spatial identity, material logic, geography, and major landmark relationships while allowing scene-appropriate camera and lighting variation.
A location change must be motivated by the approved scene rather than introduced only to make an image more visually varied.
props: Historically important or recurring props retain recognizable shape, scale, material, wear state, ownership, and continuity across scenes.
A prop must not silently change identity or historical function between adjacent scenes.

color: Derive color from period materials, location, weather, time of day, and story state instead of enforcing one project palette.
Use restrained saturation when appropriate to the historical environment, but allow justified warm, cool, bright, or dark scenes when the approved context requires them.
lighting: Prefer motivated natural, architectural, fire, candle, moon, overcast, or practical light consistent with the depicted place and period.
Lighting may shape focus and mood but should not create implausible studio spectacle or hide historically important information.
material: Surfaces, textiles, paper, wood, stone, metal, soil, vegetation, and weathering should read as physically plausible for the represented period and environment.
Avoid generic fantasy luxury, glossy game-render materials, and decorative detail unsupported by the approved reconstruction.

reconstructionEvidenceDistinction: Evidence, quoted source material, maps, documents, and artifacts must retain their source identity and should not be visually blended with generated reconstruction in a way that confuses provenance.
Generated reconstruction should be treated as explanatory visualization, not proof.
When evidence is incomplete, composition may withhold detail, use partial views, or favor contextual reconstruction instead of fabricating specific unsupported evidence.
compositionAndCameraTendencies: Favor readable story geography, clear subject hierarchy, restrained cinematic depth, and compositions that can survive editorial movement and continuity handoff.
Use camera distance and angle to support historical meaning and scene intent rather than defaulting to constant heroic close-ups.
Preserve enough environmental information in key establishing and transition images to support long-form continuity.
Avoid fixed shorts-only framing; composition is adapted by the selected format profile.
historicalUncertaintyHandling: Differentiate documented facts, reasonable reconstruction, disputed interpretation, and unknown detail in the upstream factual constraints and reflect that confidence visually.
Do not invent exact faces, inscriptions, colors, heraldry, layouts, or object details when the approved evidence does not support that specificity.
When multiple interpretations are plausible, choose a conservative representation or expose the ambiguity instead of silently selecting a sensational one.
formatAdaptationRules: The same channel Visual Bible governs LONGFORM and SHORTFORM; format-specific framing, safe areas, dimensions, and delivery constraints come from the Format Profile.
LONGFORM should prioritize sustained continuity, environmental readability, and editability across sequences.
SHORTFORM may tighten hierarchy and framing for vertical readability without changing the channel's factuality or identity rules.
avoidances: Do not inherit project-specific palettes, master images, or character identities into the channel-wide resource.
Do not use the legacy HISTORY_MYSTERY_STYLIZED_V1 master style, history_mystery_shorts_style.json, old scene prompt presets, or old master-candidate logic.
Do not treat sample markdown image style, sample palettes, or prior project artwork as authoritative style input.
Avoid anachronistic objects, fantasy costume embellishment, exaggerated caricature, game-like render language, text artifacts, watermarks, and UI unless explicitly required by an approved asset role.
